title: Normal Menstrual Cycle Length & Hormonal Physiology
sourceOrganization: World Health Organization (WHO) & International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO)
summary: Clinical parameters defining a healthy menstrual cycle: 21 to 35 days duration, bleeding lasting 2 to 7 days, and normal blood loss.
keyPoints: Normal cycle frequency: Between 21 and 35 days (measured from day 1 of one period to day 1 of the next).
Normal flow duration: Bleeding typically lasts 3 to 7 days; soaking 3 to 6 pads or tampons per day.
Ovulation (egg release) typically occurs 14 days before the onset of the next period.
Adolescent cycles in the first 1 to 2 years after menarche are frequently irregular due to maturing hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.
detailedContent: Menstruation is a healthy biological rhythm governed by cyclic rises and falls of estrogen and progesterone.
Understanding personal cycle variability empowers women to track fertility windows, identify unexpected bleeding early, and plan family goals.
whenToSeeClinician: Consult a healthcare provider if your cycle is shorter than 21 days, longer than 35 days, or if bleeding lasts longer than 8 consecutive days.
ethiopiaContext: Educational materials disseminated by the Ethiopian School Health and Nutrition Directorate.

title: Severe Menstrual Cramps (Dysmenorrhea) & Treatment
summary: Primary dysmenorrhea causes painful pelvic and back cramping due to uterine prostaglandins, responsive to NSAIDs, heat therapy, and hormonal regulation.
keyPoints: Prostaglandins cause the uterine muscle to contract and shed its lining; high levels produce intense cramping, nausea, and fatigue.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs like Ibuprofen or Mefenamic Acid) block prostaglandin synthesis most effectively when started at the very first sign of cramps.
Warm compresses or heating pads placed over the lower abdomen relax uterine smooth muscle equivalent to mild analgesics.
Secondary dysmenorrhea (caused by endometriosis, adenomyosis, or fibroids) causes chronic pain that worsens over time.
detailedContent: Severe cramps that cause school absenteeism or incapacitation are NOT something a young woman must simply endure in silence.
Combined oral contraceptive pills or hormonal IUDs significantly alleviate dysmenorrhea by thinning the endometrium and suppressing prostaglandin production.
whenToSeeClinician: Visit a health center or gynecologist if cramps do not respond to over-the-counter painkillers or if pain occurs during non-menstrual weeks or intercourse.
ethiopiaContext: Addressed in adolescent and youth-friendly services across Ethiopian high schools and universities.

title: Causes of Missed or Irregular Periods (Amenorrhea)
summary: Explores the spectrum of factors causing absent or late periods, including early pregnancy, hormonal birth control, physical/emotional stress, and PCOS.
keyPoints: Pregnancy is the most common cause of sudden missed period in sexually active women.
Hormonal methods (implants like Implanon, 3-month Depo-Provera injectables) often cause periods to become very light or pause completely without health risk.
Acute mental stress, severe caloric restriction, intensive athletics, or rapid weight shifts disrupt pituitary hormonal signals.
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) and thyroid disorders frequently present with irregular or skipped cycles.
detailedContent: Amenorrhea is categorized as primary (no period by age 15) or secondary (absence of menses for 3 months in someone who previously had periods).
Taking an over-the-counter urine pregnancy test is the essential first clinical step for sexually active individuals.
whenToSeeClinician: Take a home urine pregnancy test if your period is more than 7 days late. Visit a health center if your period is absent for 3 consecutive months.
ethiopiaContext: Confidential counseling and pregnancy testing provided free at all Kebele Health Posts in Ethiopia.

title: Reusable Medical-Grade Menstrual Cups in Schools Pilot
summary: Draft assessment of medical-grade silicone menstrual cup distribution and boiling hygiene protocols in primary and secondary schools.
keyPoints: Medical-grade silicone menstrual cups collect rather than absorb menstrual fluid, lasting up to 5 to 10 years.
Provides up to 10-12 hours of leak-free protection, reducing school absenteeism among adolescent girls.
Requires access to clean water and boiling water for sterilization between cycles.
Acceptability and peer-educator training modules currently in field trial phase.
detailedContent: Draft clinical notes: Hygiene safety monitoring and toxic shock syndrome surveillance protocols for school-based WASH interventions.
Collaborative pilot project between UNICEF Ethiopia, Ministry of Education, and regional water bureaus.
whenToSeeClinician: Speak to your school health club coordinator or health extension worker regarding proper sterilization techniques.
ethiopiaContext: Piloted across select primary and secondary schools in pastoralist and agrarian woredas in Ethiopia.
